newsitem.title: USA: Kirlin Securities pulls Sprint Spectrum bond ad.
newsitem.headline: Kirlin Securities pulls Sprint Spectrum bond ad.

text.p: Kirlin Securities Inc, a New York-based brokerage firm, has agreed to pull its ad campaign for junk bonds issued by an affiliate of Sprint Corp, according to Patrice Vellecca, director of compliance at Kirlin.

"Kirlin Securities has pulled the Sprint advertisment in its entirety and we have communicated with the company. Kirlin is also addressing this matter internally and will take appropriate action," said Vellecca, who declined further comment.

Last week, Sprint Spectrum L.P., an affiliate of Sprint Corp, asked Kirlin to stop broadcasting the ads, which included references to the long distance telephone company's familiar "pin-drop" advertising campaign and its spokewoman, Candice Bergen.
Sprint Spectrum first became aware of the ad campaign when it was brought to the company's attention by a Reuters reporter.
A spokesman for Sprint Spectrum said the ads were misleading and misrepresented the issuer of the bonds.

"Obviously, they are using some of the messages from Sprint Corp, mixed in with some of the key messages from Sprint Spectrum. We want to be sure that no one is mislead," a Sprint Spectrum spokesman said last week.
Junk bonds from Sprint Spectrum, which provides digital personal communications services, are rated "highly speculative" by major credit rating agencies.
By comparison, Sprint Corp bonds are considered "investment grade" by rating agencies.
While Sprint Spectrum is 40 percent owned by Sprint, the long-distance telephone company is not associated with Sprint Spectrum debt and has no obligation regarding its payment.
Kirlin, based in Syosset, N.Y., had been running the ad on local radio stations since June and had planned to continue the campaign for the next two weeks, according to a Kirlin official.
The firm has been the subject of various disciplinary actions in the past several years, according to the National Association of Securities Dealers.
Since 1991, Kirlin has settled in arbitration with customers three cases involving misrepresentation and suitability of securities and omission of facts, according to the NASD.
